body:
Why the 2 powers fought

Vijayanagara and the Bahmani Sultanate competed because their rulers sought control of politically and economically valuable territories. The main causes of conflict included fertile agricultural land, strategic forts, river valleys, coastal access and trading routes.

The best-known contested region was the Raichur Doab, between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers. Its agricultural productivity provided revenue, while its forts helped rulers control the territory and defend their positions.

Competition also extended towards the eastern Deccan and the Krishna–Godavari region, where fertile lands and connections to coastal commerce were important. Control of western-coast trading routes mattered because rulers needed access to valuable imports, particularly cavalry horses.

Conflict did not prevent cooperation

The political relationships among Vijayanagara, the Bahmani rulers, the Gajapatis and the later Deccan Sultanates were not permanently divided along religious lines. Rulers formed alliances, intervened in succession disputes and sometimes supported claimants in neighbouring states.

Krishnadeva Raya, for example, intervened in the affairs of neighbouring Sultanates, while rulers of Bijapur also became involved in Vijayanagara's succession politics. Competition for strategic advantages is therefore a more accurate explanation of these changing alliances than the assumption of continuous religious warfare.

Fragmentation of the Bahmani Sultanate

The Bahmani state weakened during the later 15th and early 16th centuries. Rivalries among nobles, the growing strength of provincial commanders and struggles over central authority contributed to its decline. The execution of Mahmud Gawan in 1481 removed an influential minister who had attempted to strengthen royal supervision.

Over time, the Bahmani political structure gave way to 5 principal Deccan Sultanates. Their emergence occurred over several decades rather than through a single event on one date.

AhmadnagarNizam ShahiAhmadnagar

These successor states should not be confused with the original Bahmani Sultanate. By the time of the Battle of Talikota in 1565, the principal opponents of Vijayanagara were rulers of the successor Sultanates, not a single unified Bahmani state.

The Battle of Talikota, 1565

In 1565, the Vijayanagara army, led by the powerful political figure Rama Raya, fought a combined force of Deccan Sultanates at Rakshasi-Tangadi, commonly known as Talikota.

The principal allied opponents identified in the standard account included Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda. The battle ended in a major defeat for Vijayanagara. Rama Raya was killed, and the victorious forces subsequently sacked the imperial capital.

The defeat was significant because the old capital had been a major centre of government, ceremony, commerce and imperial prestige. Its destruction undermined the political arrangements that had developed around the city.

What happened after Talikota?

The destruction of Vijayanagara city did not mean that every part of the empire ceased to exist immediately in 1565. The Aravidu dynasty continued to exercise authority from other centres, including Penukonda and later Chandragiri.

However, central control weakened, and regional military chiefs gained increasing independence. The emergence of powerful nayaka states contributed to the gradual fragmentation of the old imperial structure.

Comparing the political outcomes

The 2 states followed different paths of decline. The Bahmani Sultanate was progressively divided as provincial and dynastic powers established separate Deccan kingdoms. Vijayanagara suffered a decisive military defeat and the destruction of its principal capital in 1565, but a successor ruling line survived elsewhere.

Both histories illustrate the importance of the balance between central royal authority and powerful territorial commanders. When commanders controlled substantial military resources and revenue independently, maintaining a large kingdom became increasingly difficult.

Separate 3 historical developments

  • 1347: Foundation of the Bahmani Sultanate.
  • Late 15th–early 16th centuries: Emergence of the 5 Deccan successor Sultanates.
  • 1565: Defeat of Vijayanagara at Talikota by an alliance of Deccan Sultanates.

Prelims focus

  • Principal area of Vijayanagara–Bahmani conflict: Raichur Doab.
  • Mahmud Gawan's execution: 1481.
  • Successor Sultanates: Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Berar, Bidar and Golconda.
  • Battle of Talikota or Rakshasi-Tangadi: 1565.
  • Vijayanagara leader at Talikota: Rama Raya.
  • Trap: The Bahmani Sultanate had already fragmented before Talikota; Vijayanagara's ruling line also survived after the battle.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 7, sections 2.1–2.3 and 'Timeline 1', pp. 172–175 and 193; IGNOU, The Regional Powers: 13th–15th Century, Unit 28, sections on the Bahmani decline and successor states; NIOS, History (315), Lesson 11, sections 11.7–11.8.2. Online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]
